titre: Clausewitz (1832): War as a Politics “Mixed With Other Means”
accroche: The phrase “war is politics by other means” abridges Clausewitz: he writes that politics continues, mixed with other means.
contenu_vulgarise:
Clausewitz is summed up in one sentence: war is the continuation of politics by other means. The phrase is short, and it suggests that war takes over when politics stops. The text says the opposite, and it also says more.

## What Book VIII Says

*On War* appeared in 1832, a year after the author's death, thanks to his widow, Marie von Clausewitz. In Book VIII, chapter 6, Clausewitz presents his idea as a break with the common opinion: it is supposed, he writes, that war interrupts political relations and opens a state of affairs “subject to no law but its own.” He maintains the contrary: war is only a continuation of political relations, “with a mixture of other means.” He explains why he insists on this mixture: to assert that these relations do not cease with war, that they do not turn into something entirely different, but that they continue to exist whatever the form of the means employed. Does the cessation of diplomatic notes, he asks, stop the political relations between nations? War is “another kind of writing and language for political thoughts”: it has its own grammar, but its logic is nothing peculiar. (These quotations follow J. J. Graham's English translation, which I render here in French.)

## A Mechanism, Not a Slogan

§ 24 of Book I, chapter 1, says the same thing with a consequence for the military commander: war is “a true political instrument,” “an accomplishment of politics by other means,” and “the political point of view is the aim, war is the means, and the means must always include the aim in our conception.” The conduct of operations is therefore not a separate domain in which politicians would no longer have to intervene: the political aim gives war its character and its scale.

## The Shift

The famous phrase, taken alone, makes war a mere extension of the rulers' decision. Yet the same chapter 1 ranks politics as only one of the three tendencies that make up war: the original violence, hatred, and animosity, which can be traced to a blind instinct; the play of probabilities and chance, which makes it a free activity of the soul; and the subordinate nature of a political instrument, by which it belongs to reason alone. Clausewitz ties the first to the people, the second to the general and his army, the third to the government. Politics therefore weighs on war without fully controlling it: passions and chance have their own weight, and that is what makes war unpredictable for those who decide it.

It remains to be seen what “by other means” is worth when one of the three terms escapes the person conducting it.

repere.texte: Book VIII, chap. 6 B (translation by J. J. Graham): “war is nothing but a continuation of political intercourse, with a mixture of other means,” then: “It has certainly a grammar of its own, but its logic is not peculiar to itself.”
repere.source: Clausewitz, On War, trans. J. J. Graham, Book VIII, chap. 6 B, Project Gutenberg

carte.punch: “Politics by other means”: Clausewitz actually writes “with a mixture.”
carte.idee: For Clausewitz (1832), war does not replace politics: political relations continue during war, mixed with other means. It has its own grammar, but its logic remains that of politics.

quiz.question: What does it mean, in Clausewitz, that war is a continuation of politics “with a mixture of other means”?
choix: War begins when diplomacy fails, and politics regains its rights only at peace
Political relations do not cease during war, and the political aim determines its character
Generals must decide operations alone, since war obeys its own laws
Chance and passions have no effect once a government has set a precise objective
quiz.explication: Clausewitz rejects the idea of a break: politics continues during war and sets its aim. He does not, however, make it a pure calculation, since violence and chance also count among the three tendencies of war.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Clausewitz answer to those who believe that war ends political relations?
choix: They continue to exist, whatever the form of the means employed
They cease, then resume as soon as peace is signed
They pass into the hands of the generals, who conduct them alone
They turn into something of an entirely different nature
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Clausewitz maintains that political relations do not cease with war and do not turn into something else: only the means are mixed with violence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To which of the three tendencies of war does Clausewitz tie its nature as a political instrument?
choix: To the people, whose hatred and animosity make up the original violence
To the general and his army, who face the play of chance
To the government, through which war belongs to reason alone
To diplomacy, which negotiates the aim of war with the enemy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The people carry violence and hatred, the general and the army chance, the government reason: it is to the government that the nature of political instrument is tied.
